---
title: "Graphical Models"
---

A graphical model represents the statistical relationships among a set of
variables as a graph. Each variable is a node, and edges between nodes
encode direct statistical associations. bgms estimates undirected graphical
models — specifically, Markov Random Fields.

## Nodes and edges

In a graphical model, the $p$ variables in a dataset are represented as
nodes (or vertices) of a graph. An edge between two nodes indicates a
direct statistical association between the corresponding variables, after
accounting for all other variables in the model.

The absence of an edge between two nodes means that the two variables are
conditionally independent given the remaining variables. This is the key
interpretive property of undirected graphical models: the graph encodes the
conditional independence structure of the joint distribution.

## Conditional independence

Two variables $X_i$ and $X_j$ are conditionally independent given the rest
if knowing the value of $X_i$ provides no additional information about $X_j$
once all other variables are observed. In the graph, this corresponds to the
absence of a direct edge between nodes $i$ and $j$.

Conditional independence is distinct from marginal independence. Two variables
may be marginally correlated (both associated with a third variable) yet
conditionally independent once that third variable is accounted for. The
graphical model separates direct from indirect associations.

## Markov Random Fields

A Markov Random Field (MRF) is an undirected graphical model in which the
joint distribution of the variables factorizes according to the graph
structure. For a set of $p$ variables with observations
$\mathbf{x} = (x_1, \ldots, x_p)$, the MRF specifies:

$$
p(\mathbf{x}) \propto \exp\left(\sum_{i} \theta_i(x_i) +
\sum_{i < j} \sigma_{ij} \, s_i(x_i) \, s_j(x_j)\right)
$$

where $\theta_i(x_i)$ are main effects (node potentials), $\sigma_{ij}$ are
pairwise interaction parameters, and $s_i(x_i)$ are sufficient statistics
that depend on the variable type.

The pairwise interaction $\sigma_{ij}$ controls the edge between nodes $i$
and $j$: when $\sigma_{ij} = 0$, the edge is absent and the two variables
are conditionally independent.

## Model families in bgms

bgms supports three model families, all MRFs:

- **Ordinal MRF** — for binary and ordinal variables. Category thresholds
  serve as main effects, and pairwise interactions capture associations
  between ordinal scores. See [Ordinal MRF](omrf.qmd).

- **Gaussian Graphical Model (GGM)** — for continuous variables. The
  precision matrix (inverse covariance matrix) determines the edge
  structure: nonzero off-diagonal entries correspond to edges. See
  [GGM](ggm.qmd).

- **Mixed MRF** — for datasets containing both discrete and continuous
  variables. Combines the ordinal MRF and GGM into a joint model. See
  [Mixed MRF](mixed-model.qmd).

## Why networks?

In psychology and the social sciences, graphical models are used to study
how symptoms, attitudes, or behaviors relate to each other directly, rather
than through latent constructs. Estimating the conditional independence
structure — the network — identifies which pairs of variables have direct
associations and which are only indirectly related.

Bayesian methods add the ability to quantify evidence for the presence or
absence of each edge, rather than relying on thresholding rules applied to
point estimates. bgms implements this through Bayesian edge selection with
spike-and-slab priors (see [Edge Selection](edge-selection.qmd)).
